context: baggage-handling & security-led · large-volume HVAC under a long-span roof

brief.intro: New to this project type? An airport passenger terminal is a large-span public building whose real complexity is not the shell but the systems that move bags and people safely and quickly: the Baggage Handling System (BHS), security screening, and large-volume air conditioning. The structure — piled foundations and a long-span roof with no internal columns — is a big, visible package, but it is not what makes the programme hard. Your schedule stands or falls on getting the BHS and security systems designed, procured and integrated in time, and on the terminal opening in coordinated zones (a pier or level at a time) rather than as one single date.

scope.name: Enabling & site works
scope.desc: Earthworks, piling mobilisation, apron-tie-in grading, landside road interface.

scope.name: Structure & long-span roof
scope.desc: Piled foundations, steel or concrete frame, and the wide-span roof trusses that keep the halls column-free.

scope.name: Building envelope
scope.desc: Curtain wall, roof cladding and glazing — getting the terminal weather-tight.

scope.name: Baggage Handling System (BHS)
scope.desc: Conveyors, sortation, and inline explosive-detection screening (EDS) moving bags from check-in to aircraft.

scope.name: Security & access control
scope.desc: Screening checkpoints, CCTV, access control and the landside/airside boundary.

scope.name: Mechanical — HVAC & chilled water
scope.desc: Large-volume air handling for departure/arrival halls, chilled-water plant, and smoke-control fans.

scope.name: Electrical power & lighting
scope.desc: Incoming substations, standby generation, and terminal, retail and apron-facing lighting.

scope.name: Fire & life safety
scope.desc: Fire alarm, sprinkler/wet risers, voice evacuation and the smoke-control system that protects large open halls.

scope.name: Passenger ELV / IT systems
scope.desc: Flight information display (FIDS), public address, wayfinding, and structured cabling/data.

scope.name: Interior fit-out & finishes
scope.desc: Flooring, ceilings, check-in and retail counters — the last layer before opening.

glossary.plain: baggage handling system — the conveyor network that sorts bags from check-in to the aircraft.
explosive detection system — the screening machines bags pass through inside the BHS.
the arrival/departure screens showing flight information.
the paved area where aircraft park and are serviced.
the walkway that connects the terminal to the aircraft door.
landside is the public area before security; airside is the secure zone after screening.
systems that clear smoke and guide passengers safely out of large open halls in a fire.
a wide-span structure with no internal columns, covering large open halls.

must_get_right: The BHS and security screening systems drive the fit-out programme — order and commission them early; they are the true critical path, not the shell.
Protect the landside/airside boundary — security & access control must be tested and locked down before any phased opening.
Large-volume HVAC and smoke control need the roof and envelope fully weather-tight before ductwork balancing and life-safety testing can start.
A terminal opens pier-by-pier or level-by-level, not on one date — break the schedule into handover zones from day one.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual and phased-opening milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Structure and envelope run a 6-day week; MEP and BHS fit-out move to two shifts at peak to protect the opening date; any works within live apron or landside operating areas are restricted to approved airport-authority access windows.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs BHS/security long-lead procurement → structure & roof weather-tight → BHS and security install → controls integration → integrated fire/life-safety and BHS throughput testing → phased zone handover. The long-span roof erection and the BHS procurement-to-install chain are the two activities most likely to control the finish date — name both explicitly when reviewing progress.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen and authority approvals obtained per phase gate; the terminal opens in coordinated zones (pier or level) rather than as a single date; a single mobilisation; and the client free-issues no equipment. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Apron-side works are coordinated with live or phased airport operations; laydown for BHS and long-span steel is constrained by the building footprint; specialist BHS and security-integration subcontractors are scarce and often shared across zones.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: BHS commissioning re-test loops, security-systems integration slippage, and weather risk to long-span roof erection. Schedule contingency is held immediately before the integrated fire/life-safety test and before each zone's phased handover rather than spread thinly across activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
